title: Technology Diffusion and Polycrisis Resilience
subtitle: Accelerating the Adoption of Technologies That Reduce Global Vulnerability
description: A foundational monograph establishing that accelerating the global diffusion of technologies that reduce human and systemic vulnerability is a fundamental…
contribution: Develops the Technology Diffusion and Polycrisis Resilience framework—originated by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics—demonstrating that humanity's resilience depends not only on what technologies it invents, but on how rapidly, affordably, and equitably it deploys vulnerability-reducing technologies worldwide.
abstract:
Technology Diffusion and Polycrisis Resilience is a foundational publication within the H Heuristics Polycrisis Resilience Series, based on the concept developed by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics (https://polycrisisresilience.hheuristics.com/).
It develops a unified framework connecting technological innovation, international technology transfer, affordability, infrastructure development, institutional capacity, and economic convergence to the broader objective of reducing global vulnerability.

keyFindings.title: Accelerating the global diffusion of technologies that reduce human and systemic vulnerability is a fundamental mechanism for strengthening Polycrisis Resilience; innovation alone does not build resilience until adoption reaches vulnerable populations at scale.

Humanity's resilience depends not only on what technologies it develops, but on how effectively it distributes and deploys technologies capable of improving human development and strengthening interconnected systems across energy, health, agriculture, water, and digital infrastructure.
Financial, infrastructural, institutional, and tariff barriers currently create up to 24 years of cumulative adoption lag between frontier invention and last-mile deployment in low-income economies.

Treating technology diffusion as a central global resilience strategy compresses systemic vulnerability from 66.0 (2025) to 21.5 by 2050 and 8.5 by 2100 (-87.1%), delivering 7.4x–11.6x social benefit-cost ratios.
